lines.text: The farm was a cavern as big as Greyhollow's whole valley. And it was quiet. That was the worst of it. It was so quiet.
The walls were cut into alcoves, thousands of them, rising into the dark like a honeycomb. And in every alcove, someone was asleep.
Children. Old men. Women my father's age. Each one lying on a bed of pale glass, with a stone on their chest.
And on every stone, a crystal was growing. Milky white, with a faint light inside it, like a pulse.
Hollow-born, every one. Springs, like you, Lucan. A spring never runs dry. So the Order keeps them asleep, and lets them pour into stone. Forever.
At the far end, two Measurers in grey aprons walked the rows with silver shears, snipping off the crystals and dropping them in baskets, like men picking apples.
Wren added them to her list.
Beyond them was a workshop. Benches and tools, and racks of finished work shining under the lamps.
Rings. Hundreds of rings, all of milky glass. And rows of little white vials, exactly like the one at my brother's throat.
Penhallow's ring. Fane's. Caddoc's gauntlets. The Stone they used on you. Maric's draught. It all comes from here.
Every five-ring heir in the Highmarket. Every ring that ever flickered. All of it was people, sleeping in the dark under the cathedral.
In the Deep, we had sealed up a wall of frozen people, so that nobody would ever cut them for glass. Skeld law. My law.
The Order had found a way around it. It didn't cut people into glass. It grew them.
And I understood what the Order had always wanted with me. Not a cell. A bed. One more alcove in the honeycomb, for the biggest spring they had ever found.
Ash had wandered to the nearest alcove, where a little boy lay asleep. He pushed his nose into the boy's cold hand, the way he does with me when I'm sad.
The boy didn't wake. But in his sleep, very slightly, he smiled.
Tamsin was gone. She was running from alcove to alcove, holding her lamp up to every small face. Not that one. Not that one. Not that one.
She'd be nine now. Copper hair. Freckles. She'd be nine.
Then, at the very end of the last row, she stopped.
Someone had scratched a bird into the stone beside an alcove. Then another. And another. Hundreds of little birds, all over the wall, all flying the same way.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred, coming soon.
